A valve that matches the pipe can still be the wrong valve. The diameter tells you the size of the opening; the numbers that matter describe behaviour under load. Verify a short list instead.
Maximum flow capacity.
Peak morning demand across a riser must pass freely. A valve sized to average demand throttles every fixture at the busiest hour.
Pressure-drop characteristics.
A restrictive valve costs pressure at every fixture downstream, and tenants notice.
Actuator fail-safe behaviour.
Decide in advance whether a power loss leaves the valve open or closed, and tell the people who respond.

The running toilet in the table moves about a gallon an hour. A sensor tuned only for large flows will never close on it.

Remote closure is only as good as the link that carries the command.

What to test before you trust it

Commissioning is where claims become facts. Run a sustained low-flow event and see whether the valve treats it as a leak or ignores it. Open a high-flow rupture and measure time to closure. Where It Fits in Multifamily, Condominium and Commercial Buildings

At 2 a.m. in a 60-suite building, a fitting on a riser in the ground-floor mechanical room starts to weep. Nobody is awake. Water is already tracking along the slab toward the elevator lobby, and the first person to notice will be a resident on the floor below, barefoot, at breakfast.

Now run the same night with a sensor on the mechanical-room floor and a valve on the building supply. The alert reaches the on-call number within minutes, the valve closes, and the water stops at the source before it reaches the corridor. The cleanup is a wet mechanical room rather than three suites and a lobby.

children.text: Placement decides what gets protected

Building-level closure protects every riser downstream, which is what you want for a main break and what you don't want for a false alarm at 9 a.m. on a Tuesday. A branch valve isolates one zone or one suite riser, so a closure affects a defined group of occupants rather than everyone.

Sensors belong where water collects. Mechanical rooms, laundry rooms, water-heater closets, under sink cabinets in suites and common-area restrooms carry most of the risk, which is why the sensor map should be drawn before any valve is specified.

Suite meters add a second, independent view. Unusually high consumption on one meter can flag a slow leak that never trips a floor sensor, while the shutoff log helps validate what the meter recorded during the event. Neither instrument covers the other's blind spot on its own.
For buildings where closures must be coordinated with staff, this short walkthrough of how a leak triggers a closure is worth watching before you write a procedure.

Mixed-use properties raise the stakes, because one domestic supply often feeds retail units, common washrooms and residential risers from the same main. Closing that main to protect a mechanical room can shut a café during trading hours. The design answer is usually zone valves with independent sensors, not a single whole-building trip.

The occupant side needs a written answer before installation, not after. Who holds authority to reopen the supply, how tenants are notified when water is off, what happens when a false alarm closes a line during a working day, and how long a suite can be without water before it becomes a habitability issue. Put those four answers in the operations manual and give the on-call contact a paper copy.
What the Valve Cannot Do and What Claims to Test

Start with the gap. A valve responds only to water at the points it can see, so anything downstream of an unmonitored branch runs unseen. Drain-side failures are outside its scope entirely, and slow seepage that never crosses a threshold can continue for weeks.
Three corrections are worth making before you sign anything.
It doesn't replace inspection.
Fittings, risers, appliance hoses and water-heater pans still need eyes on them. The valve limits the consequence of a failure, it doesn't prevent the failure.
The headline percentage is a manufacturer claim.
Moen announced an agreement with Frontdoor

to install its Flo Smart Water Monitor and Shutoff for California customers who obtain the device through certain home-insurance marketing programs. The announcement cited a potential reduction in water-damage claim frequency of as much as
, which is a manufacturer-reported performance claim, not an independent statewide result.
There is no broad statewide code mandate.

California adoption is insurer- and program-driven rather than a universal legal requirement, so treat any claim that the state building code requires smart shutoff valves cautiously unless an official code provision says so.

That second point matters commercially as well as technically. A number produced by a manufacturer tells you what the product can do under favourable conditions. It doesn't tell you what your building will achieve, because outcomes depend on where sensors sit, how the threshold is set, whether the valve closes reliably under load, how fast the response is, and whether the leak happens upstream or downstream of the monitored point. Some qualifying devices only flag abnormal use while others provide remote closure, and it's worth knowing which one sits in your budget.
If the priority is preventing water from reaching finished space at all,
flood prevention measures
that combine detection with building-level isolation outperform any single device.
Treat every vendor figure as a hypothesis you test against your own baseline, alert log and closure record.
Confirm Local Rules and Insurance Terms Before You Buy

The purchase order is the wrong place to discover a constraint. A valve that fails a rebate's approved-product list, a pipe run with no room for the tap point, or a program that excludes your building type can each stop a project after the money is committed. Work through the following checks before any equipment is specified, and get the answers in writing.
Installation point.
Confirm whether a qualifying device must sit inline on the cold-water main after the meter and the primary shutoff, and who signs off on the tap point.
Who fits it.
Professional installation may be a condition of the rebate, the warranty and the insurance credit.
Network and power.
Many devices depend on reliable Wi-Fi for remote closure and alerts. Ask what still works when the connection drops.
Property eligibility.
Some programs are limited to single-family customers rather than multifamily buildings, which rules out most strata and apartment owners.
Budget.
Rebate values differ by agency.
SoCal Water$mart
starts at $100 and depends on the participating agency and its approved-product list, and agency device listings run from roughly
before tax and shipping. For CalWEP's 2025 rebate programme through participating agencies, gather receipts, model information and proof of service address before applying.
Insurance credit.
Ask your insurer whether the device qualifies for underwriting credit rather than assuming a discount. LexisNexis estimates cited by
Parks Associates
put water-leak damage at twice the rate of fire or theft events and suggest prevention may reduce average claim payouts by
, though those are portfolio-level estimates rather than a promise about your building.

After installation, record the evidence that supports your renewal conversation: baseline consumption, alert frequency, closure events, false positives, restoration time and incidents avoided. A month of normal readings gives you the denominator every leak claim needs. Without it, you cannot show how much water an undetected leak would have lost before closure, or whether the valve's response time limited the volume that escaped. One building's records are more persuasive than any brochure.

For owners who want detection built into the metering scope, Axis Meter Solutions installs leak detection sensors in high-risk areas during metering installation. The sensors monitor the building 24/7 and alert the customer immediately when water is detected where it should not be, with placement near water heaters, under sinks, in laundry rooms, in mechanical rooms and in common areas. A water submeter alone does not detect every possible leak. Consumption data reveals unusual usage patterns, dedicated sensors detect water at selected locations, and a combined design gives broader protection than either one alone. Coverage questions of this kind are operational rather than legal advice, so local requirements still need confirmation before meters are purchased, installed or used for occupant billing.
Write the checklist this week, collect four weeks of baseline consumption, and ask one provider to state their detection coverage in writing, room by room.

Every Axis Meter Solutions installation includes leak and flood detection at no extra cost, covering mechanical rooms, laundry rooms, under-sink cabinets and common areas with sensors monitored 24/7 and an immediate alert the moment water appears where it should not. Axis owns and maintains the equipment, keeps the sensors and batteries serviced through the term, and pairs suite-level consumption data with dedicated leak detection so a slow leak surfaces as a pattern change before it becomes a repair bill.   • Who fits it. Professional installation may be a condition of the rebate, the warranty and the insurance credit.
  • Network and power. Many devices depend on reliable Wi-Fi for remote closure and alerts. Ask what still works when the connection drops.
  • Property eligibility. Some programs are limited to single-family customers rather than multifamily buildings, which rules out most strata and apartment owners.
  • Budget. Rebate values differ by agency. SoCal Water$mart starts at $100 and depends on the participating agency and its approved-product list, and agency device listings run from roughly $393 to $613 before tax and shipping. For CalWEP's 2025 rebate programme through participating agencies, gather receipts, model information and proof of service address before applying.
  • Insurance credit. Ask your insurer whether the device qualifies for underwriting credit rather than assuming a discount. LexisNexis estimates cited by Parks Associates put water-leak damage at twice the rate of fire or theft events and suggest prevention may reduce average claim payouts by 72%, though those are portfolio-level estimates rather than a promise about your building.

After installation, record the evidence that supports your renewal conversation: baseline consumption, alert frequency, closure events, false positives, restoration time and incidents avoided. A month of normal readings gives you the denominator every leak claim needs. Without it, you cannot show how much water an undetected leak would have lost before closure, or whether the valve's response time limited the volume that escaped. One building's records are more persuasive than any brochure.

For owners who want detection built into the metering scope, Axis Meter Solutions installs leak detection sensors in high-risk areas during metering installation. The sensors monitor the building 24/7 and alert the customer immediately when water is detected where it should not be, with placement near water heaters, under sinks, in laundry rooms, in mechanical rooms and in common areas. A water submeter alone does not detect every possible leak. Consumption data reveals unusual usage patterns, dedicated sensors detect water at selected locations, and a combined design gives broader protection than either one alone. Coverage questions of this kind are operational rather than legal advice, so local requirements still need confirmation before meters are purchased, installed or used for occupant billing.

Write the checklist this week, collect four weeks of baseline consumption, and ask one provider to state their detection coverage in writing, room by room.
